Day 57 of 100 · Networking Deep Dive

TLS 1.3 Handshake

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityNetworking Deep DivePublished artifact recovered

Before encrypted application traffic starts, TLS negotiates keys and lets the client validate the server certificate chain and requested hostname.

Architecture / mental model

ClientHello(SNI,key share) → ServerHello → certificate + proof → Finished ⇄ encrypted application traffic

How it works

A simplified TLS 1.3 handshake begins with ClientHello parameters such as supported protocol versions and key share, usually including the requested hostname through SNI.

The server selects parameters, sends its certificate chain and proves possession of the corresponding private key. The client validates hostname, validity period, signatures and a chain terminating at a trusted certificate.

After handshake completion, HTTP or another application protocol travels using negotiated traffic keys. If TLS terminates at a reverse proxy, the proxy-to-origin leg becomes a separate security decision.

Hands-on reference

openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com -showcerts
curl -Iv https://example.com

Verification

Check the requested hostname, certificate subject/SANs, issuer chain and verification result. Test SNI explicitly when multiple hostnames share an endpoint.

Field note / gotcha

A server can present a valid leaf certificate and still fail clients if it does not provide the intermediate chain needed to build trust.

Security considerations

Protect private keys, renew certificates before expiry, secure proxy-to-origin traffic when it crosses an untrusted network and do not weaken verification to silence errors.

What I learned

The browser padlock describes channel protection, not a background check on the site operator.
